source.title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Superposition

page_placements.theme: Superposition geometry, adversarial vulnerability and robustness

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses toy models based on Elhage et al. and measures features per dimension against feature sparsity, including an appendix reproduction of the Elhage-style experiment. It also extends the experiments with gradient attacks, adversarial training, and ResNet18 analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports toy-model results on sparsity, features per dimension, adversarial vulnerability, and interference geometry; these are recorded below. It also reports a ResNet18 SAE-reconstruction result and layer-by-layer L0 measurements for adversarial versus clean images. Theoretical explanations and cited findings from other papers are not recorded as results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces the Elhage et al. toy model (n=100 features, m=20 hidden) and sweeps sparsity. It reports features per dimension rising with sparsity, an antipodal plateau, and transitions near 1/(1-S) ≈ 1.7 and ≈ 4 (Fig 2A, Fig 7A). That is the same method and measure as V1's original. Its main focus, adversarial vulnerability and adversarial training, measures a different construct and does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that superposition is at least one causal factor in adversarial examples, possibly the primary one. In toy models, superposition controls robustness and robustness controls superposition. In ResNet18, robustness lowers an SAE-loss proxy for superposition. They acknowledge reliance on proxies and that they cannot isolate superposition's contribution in real models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a simplified Elhage-style toy-model setup and the features-per-dimension measure, and includes an appendix reproduction of the Elhage-style attack experiment. The main experiments use a noise-plus-gradient L2 attack and add adversarial-training interventions; real-model measurements use ResNet18 and SAE loss proxies.
record.method_sensitivity: The toy-model vulnerability curve includes a dip around antipodal superposition; the paper also reports that models with similar overall superposition can differ in vulnerability depending on superposition structure. FGSM and PGD produce different layer-wise L0 patterns in ResNet18.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy models, one-step gradient L2 adversarial vulnerability rises with sparsity and features per dimension. Vulnerability dips at antipodal superposition. Under Elhage-style attacks, the correlation with features per dimension is r≈0.99.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy models, adversarial vulnerability scales with the degree of superposition.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial training lowers features per dimension at fixed sparsity and lowers vulnerability. Non-robust models show about 2× the off-diagonal interference of robust ones, with similar graph geometry.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial training reduces superposition in toy models while preserving its geometric structure.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarially trained ResNet18 models get lower TopK SAE reconstruction loss at fixed k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness is associated with lower SAE loss, read by the authors as a proxy for less superposition.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial images activate more SAE features than clean ones in ResNet18. PGD reaches 2.8× at layer4, while FGSM is near baseline at layer4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial attacks increase the number of active SAE features, depending on layer and attack type.

record.problems: The authors state that they cannot directly manipulate superposition in real models, so the ResNet18 result relies on SAE loss as a proxy. The toy-model comparison across feature densities changes the evaluation distribution. The text gives qualitative trends for several plotted results without exact values; the reported L0 table does include SEMs.

untested.parts: Varying feature importance is not tested (uniform importance only). Near-orthogonality of stored directions and regular polytope geometry are not quantified; the graphs are qualitative.
All of it: no neuron polysemanticity or importance-based capacity allocation.
All of it: no LLMs. The SAE work is on ResNet18 and serves as a proxy.
All of it: SAEs are used as a proxy tool, not tested for completeness or stability.
All of it: no comparison between one-dimensional and multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Replication of the Elhage experiment: features per dimension vs 1/(1-S), with transitions at about 1.7 (onset of superposition) and about 4 (beyond antipodal). This directly bears on V1's sparsity-dependent transition.
Correlation between features per dimension and Elhage-style attack vulnerability, r≈0.99, p<0.0001 (a vulnerability result, not a version).

record.verdict_notes: V1 is supported only by the reproduction part of the study; the adversarial findings are a different construct. R2–R7 were relinked to none. A revision note says a plotting bug in Figure 6 exaggerated the clean vs adversarial L0 gap. Table 2 values are the corrected numbers, and the text's 1.3× FGSM conv1 ratio is consistent with them.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report feature-importance variation; its toy models use uniform feature importance. It measures superposition with features per dimension and interference geometry, but does not establish that all stored directions are nearly orthogonal.
The study does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared neuron capacity.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The real models studied are ResNet18s, not LLMs. SAE reconstruction and feature-activation counts do not test whether LLM activations are distributed across neurons or recoverable as sparse dictionary features.
The study uses SAE loss as a proxy for superposition, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of a model's representation.
The study describes features as directions in its toy-model setup but does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

statements.correction: Appendix A, Figure 7B: Elhage-style attacks; vulnerability versus features per dimension r≈0.99, p<0.0001. Sections 3.2–3.3, Figure 2B: noise-plus-gradient attacks; vulnerability dip at antipodal superposition.
statements.problem: The correlation is explicitly reported for Elhage-style attacks, but the cited rows and explicit textual report of the antipodal dip concern noise-plus-gradient attacks. The text does not establish the dip under Elhage-style attacks.
